collection_summary: This instance is a curated, source-defined ground truth listing the 13 MOOC-provider platforms appearing in Wikipedia's 'List of MOOC providers' master article that have their own dedicated English Wikipedia article, were founded between 2000 and 2020 inclusive (per the per-platform Wikipedia article, which is preferred over the master-list 'Founded' column when the two disagree), were currently operating at the snapshot date (2026-05-01, re-validated 2026-05-06), AND have a Founders cell that can be source-grounded from the cited per-platform article via either an explicit Founders/Founder(s)/Created-by infobox field or a body-text 'founded by' / 'co-founded by' / 'created by' / 'initiated by' / 'launched by' / 'founding partners' verb-phrase. Each row's cells trace to that platform's Wikipedia article (lead paragraph + infobox).
source_coverage_notes:
Roles:
- source_urls[0] (List_of_MOOC_providers): universe + filter (the master article's wikitable enumerates the canonical MOOC providers; the 13 staged rows are exactly the providers from this list that satisfy the 5-clause filter — own English Wikipedia article, founded 2000-2020 per the per-platform article, currently operating, B2C primary, AND Founders cell source-groundable from the per-platform article)
- source_urls[1..13] (13 per-platform Wikipedia articles, alphabetical by platform): entity-detail + value (each platform's article supplies that platform's Founded, Founders, and Country of Origin cells; cells are taken from the article's lead paragraph + infobox cross-reference). The per-platform article is also the authoritative source for the founding-year filter when the master list's 'Founded' column disagrees — see the cycle-9 Stanford Online case (master 2006 vs per-platform 1995) and the OUA case (master 2013 vs per-platform 1993) in decision_log, plus the three retained discrepancies (Khan Academy, OpenClassrooms, Udacity) documented in the cycle-10 decision_log entry.
- source_urls[14] (Wikimedia_Foundation): supporting source for Wikiversity's Country of Origin (added in cycle 10). The Wikiversity Wikipedia article infobox supplies `Owner: Wikimedia Foundation` but does not directly state a country/HQ; the Wikimedia Foundation article supplies 'Headquartered in San Francisco, California, United States', which grounds the staged Wikiversity Country of Origin = United States via the explicit owner→parent derivation chain.

No separate validation source. Each per-platform article is the canonical source for that platform's row; cell-level audit can spot-check by reading the lead paragraph of the cited article. The 'Massive open online course' overview article that anchored cycles 1-7 was dropped from the source plan in cycle 8 because under MOOC-only scope the master 'List of MOOC providers' article is itself the canonical universe-and-conceptual anchor — the conceptual MOOC overview adds no incremental sourcing role.
decision_log:
Candidate card (per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: Pass. Universe (MOOC-provider platforms with own English Wikipedia article, founded 2000-2020, currently operating, source-grounded Founders) is fully source-defined via the 5-clause filter applied to a structured Wikipedia source-list; partition rule (per platform) is source-defined; per-platform attribute cells are source-defined via each platform's Wikipedia article (lead + infobox). Table is LLM-knowable for a pre-2025 cutoff: top platforms (Coursera, Khan Academy, edX, Udemy, Udacity) are very memorable with founder names well-known; mid-pack (FutureLearn, OpenClassrooms, Alison) moderately known; tail (Shaw Academy, Wikiversity, Kadenze, iversity, SWAYAM) tests calibration. Row count (13) is comfortably above the 10-row gate. Confidence gradient is real (Coursera/Khan Academy founders very memorable; FutureLearn's 12 founding partners and Wikiversity's Wikimedia community attribution less memorable in cell-level retrieval).
- Seed/provenance: original instance, not derived from a seed in example_questions.txt. Picker recommended an original Education instance to plant the lone remaining family-level gap.
- Category: multi_attribute_projection (gap 3) primary; temporal (gap 4) secondary because the founding-year column gives a meaningful 2006-2017 axis. The DB-analog shape is a multi-column SELECT over the per-platform set, exactly matching multi_attribute_projection's canonical projection primitive.
- Source plan: Tier B Wikipedia, source_count = 15 (1 master MOOC-providers article + 13 per-platform articles + 1 Wikimedia Foundation supporting article for Wikiversity's country derivation, added in cycle 10); gt_construction = manual_wikipedia.
- Expected shape: 13 rows x 4 columns; PK = Platform.
- Domain: Education/EdTech — first instance in the Education family.
- Risks/adaptation: per-platform infobox label heterogeneity made fully-automated extraction unreliable so cells are hand-curated from per-platform Wikipedia articles. The 2000-2020 founding-year window is a curator-imposed normalization clause.
- Decision: Stage.

Why original rather than seed-driven: no seed in example_questions.txt targets education or online learning; an original Education-family instance was the highest-priority pick per the 2026-05-01 picker snapshot.

Why this Education-family shape rather than alternatives: four candidate Education shapes were considered: (a) tertiary attainment >50% (set_filter, OECD-skewed), (b) THE world university rankings top 30 (top_k, ranking-controversy), (c) oldest universities in continuous operation (set_filter, historical canon), and (d) major B2C online learning platforms (multi_attribute_projection, modern angle). The user chose (d) because it avoids both Nobel-and-laureates and country-attribute clichés and uses the multi-Wikipedia-per-entity sourcing pattern that worked well for prior multi-source instances.

Category <-> operation_type pairing: query_category=multi_attribute_projection pairs canonically with operation_type=projection per references/artifact-contract.md. The 3-attribute SELECT per row (Founded, Founders, Country of Origin) is the canonical multi-attribute projection structure (1 key + ≥3 non-key cells meets the protocol minimum).

Domain selection: Education/EdTech is the first instance in the Education family.

Post-audit cycles 1-7 history (compressed): cycles 1-2 added missing master-list entries (Alison, OpenClassrooms, Kadenze, OpenLearning, SWAYAM, Unacademy, iversity, FUN, openHPI) and corrected per-row value mismatches (Babbel founders 2→4, Memrise 2→3, Brilliant 2013→2012, Lingoda 2013→2012). Cycles 3-5 hardened the source-grounded-Founders policy: cycle 3 dropped FUN (Owner-only), cycle 4 adopted strict policy and dropped openHPI (Owner-only) while extending FutureLearn from 1 institutional founder to all 12 founding partners, cycle 5 dropped OpenLearning (Key people outside strict policy) and extended XuetangX from 1 institutional founder to both founders. Cycle 6 was a hygiene pass for narrative drift. Cycle 7 raised one BLOCKING about universe definition: the 'cross-referenced language-learning / coding / skills / K-12 / test-prep / tech-skills' subcategory clause had no canonical Wikipedia source-list anchor — it was effectively curator-defined.

Post-audit (2026-05-01, cycle 8): the cycle-7 BLOCKING was resolved by Path B re-scope to MOOC-providers-only. The universe is now exactly the entries on the 'List of MOOC providers' master wikitable that pass the 5-clause filter. Eighteen platforms from the cycle-7 universe were dropped: 17 non-MOOC platforms (Babbel, Brilliant, Busuu, Codecademy, CreativeLive, Duolingo, freeCodeCamp, Lingoda, Magoosh, MasterClass, Memrise, Outschool, Pluralsight, Quizlet, Skillshare, Treehouse, Unacademy) — none appear on the master list — and one non-master-list MOOC (XuetangX). Three master-list entries that pass the strict 5-clause filter were added: Shaw Academy, Stanford Online, Wikiversity. Eight other master-list entries fail the strict filter and were documented as exclusions: Canvas Network (no own English Wikipedia article), MIT OpenCourseWare ('initiative of MIT' is institutional but outside the strict-policy verb-phrase list), OpenSAP ('provided by SAP' similarly outside the verb-phrase list), Open Universities Australia (founded 1993, pre-2000), Saylor Academy (founded 1999, pre-2000), France Université Numérique (Owner-only, retired in cycle 3), openHPI (Owner-only, retired in cycle 4), and OpenLearning (Key people only, retired in cycle 5). The 'Primary Content Domain' column was dropped because under MOOC-only scope every row would have Domain = 'MOOC' (zero calibration capacity); the schema is now 4 columns, which still meets the multi_attribute_projection 1-key + ≥3-non-key minimum. Net cycle-8 universe: 29 → 14. The 'Massive open online course' overview article was dropped from source_urls (its conceptual-anchor role is now redundant given the master MOOC-providers list IS the conceptual+universe anchor). source_count went from 31 (cycle 7) to 15 (cycle 8 — 1 master + 14 per-platform). The trade-off is platform diversity (down from 10 content domains to 1 content domain) for source-defined rigor (the universe rule is now anchored to a single structured Wikipedia source-list rather than a curator-assembled subcategory union).

Post-audit (2026-05-06, cycle 9): the cycle-8 audit raised one BLOCKING and one NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE. (a) BLOCKING — Stanford Online founded-year discrepancy: cycle-8 staged Stanford Online with Founded = 2006 (the value in the master 'List of MOOC providers' table). On re-investigation, the per-platform Stanford Online Wikipedia article body explicitly says 'Stanford Online was founded in 1995 through the Stanford Center for Professional Development, [...] it has a history that spans back to the late 1960s'. Under the per-platform-article-preferred normalization rule (codified in cycle 2 and applied consistently to other master-vs-per-platform discrepancies including OpenLearning's 2012-vs-2013 case and Open Universities Australia's 2013-vs-1993 case), the per-platform article wins; Stanford Online's true founding year is 1995, which fails the 2000-2020 filter. Resolved by dropping Stanford Online from the staged set and adding it to the documented pre-2000 exclusion list with explicit master-vs-per-platform-discrepancy framing. (b) NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE — exclusion documentation drift: The Great Courses (founded 1990 per master list, also 1990 per per-platform article) and LinkedIn Learning (founded 1995 per both master and per-platform article — formerly Lynda.com, rebranded after the 2015 LinkedIn acquisition) are master-list entries that fail the pre-2000 founding-year filter but were not enumerated in the prior exclusion documentation. Both added to the documented pre-2000 exclusion list. Net universe after cycle 9: 14 → 13. Country distribution after Stanford Online drop: United States 7 (Coursera, edX, Kadenze, Khan Academy, Udacity, Udemy, Wikiversity), Ireland 2 (Alison, Shaw Academy), United Kingdom 1 (FutureLearn), Germany 1 (iversity), France 1 (OpenClassrooms), India 1 (SWAYAM). source_count 15 → 14 (Stanford_Online URL removed from source_urls). Master-list completeness state: 24 master-list entries total = 13 staged + 11 documented exclusions split across 3 failure classes (5 source-grounded-Founders failures + 1 own-article failure + 5 pre-2000 founding-year failures, with Stanford Online newly added to the pre-2000 class in this cycle).

Post-audit (2026-05-11, cycle 10): the cycle-9 audit raised one BLOCKING and one NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE. (a) BLOCKING — Wikiversity Country of Origin not source-grounded: cycle-8/9 staging assigned Wikiversity Country = United States, but the Wikiversity Wikipedia article does not directly state a country or headquarters; its infobox supplies only `Owner: Wikimedia Foundation` and `Created by: Wikimedia community`. The US derivation comes from the Wikimedia Foundation's San Francisco HQ, which is sourced from the Wikimedia Foundation Wikipedia article — but that article was not in source_urls. Resolved by adding `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikimedia_Foundation` to source_urls (source_count 14 → 15), with the explicit derivation chain documented in source_coverage_notes and normalization_decisions: Wikiversity infobox `Owner: Wikimedia Foundation` → Wikimedia Foundation article 'Headquartered in San Francisco, California, United States' → staged Country of Origin = United States. (b) NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE — under-documented retained master-vs-per-platform 'Founded' discrepancies AND stale cycle-8 wording in the candidate card. In addition to the two pre-2000 discrepancies that pulled rows out of the staged set (Stanford Online, Open Universities Australia), three retained rows have master-vs-per-platform 'Founded' value disagreements that the per-platform-preferred rule resolves silently: (i) Khan Academy — master list 2006 vs per-platform infobox `Launched: 2008`; staged 2008 (per-platform preferred). (ii) OpenClassrooms — master list 2007 vs per-platform article internal split (infobox `Launched: 10 November 1999` for the original Site du Zéro entity; article lead 'Founded in 2013 by Pierre Dubuc and Mathieu Nebra, OpenClassrooms…' for the OpenClassrooms-brand rebrand); staged 2013 follows the lead's brand-founding framing. The Stanford-Online-vs-OpenClassrooms asymmetry is genuine: Stanford Online's article body has a single 'Stanford Online was founded in 1995' statement with no competing rebrand-year framing in the lead, while OpenClassrooms's article lead explicitly says 'Founded in 2013… OpenClassrooms' (brand-founding-year framing) and the 1999 infobox value refers to the pre-rebrand entity Site du Zéro — so the lead's 2013 wins under the lead+infobox preferred rule. (iii) Udacity — master list 2012 vs per-platform infobox internal split (`Founded: June 2011` corporate founding vs `Launched: February 2012` product launch); staged 2011 prefers the `Founded` field as the more conventional sense of 'founding year'. Candidate card wording updated from cycle-8 '14 rows / 15 sources' to current '13 rows / 15 sources' (the source_count is back to 15 in cycle 10 because the Wikimedia Foundation URL replaces what Stanford Online's URL gave in cycle 8). Net cycle-10 universe: 13 → 13 (no row changes; only source_count +1 for the Wikimedia Foundation addition and narrative-completeness corrections).
normalization_decisions: Universe definition: the staged universe is the entries on Wikipedia's 'List of MOOC providers' master wikitable that pass all five filter clauses simultaneously: (1) own dedicated English Wikipedia article (Canvas Network fails — redirects to Instructure), (2) founded between 2000 and 2020 inclusive per the per-platform Wikipedia article (with the per-platform article preferred over the master-list 'Founded' column when the two disagree — Stanford Online (master 2006 vs per-platform 1995) and Open Universities Australia (master 2013 vs per-platform 1993) are the two filter-pulling discrepancies — i.e., the two master-vs-per-platform 'Founded' disagreements where the per-platform value falls pre-2000 and excludes the row from the staged set; three additional retained-row 'Founded' discrepancies (Khan Academy, OpenClassrooms, Udacity) are documented later in this section, where the per-platform-preferred rule quietly overrides the master-list value without changing row membership), (3) currently operating at the snapshot date, (4) B2C primary, AND (5) Founders cell source-groundable from the per-platform Wikipedia article via either an explicit `Founders` / `Founder(s)` / `Created by` infobox field OR a body-text 'founded by' / 'co-founded by' / 'created by' / 'initiated by' / 'launched by' / 'founding partners' verb-phrase clause (FUN, openHPI, OpenLearning, MIT OpenCourseWare, OpenSAP fail this clause — see exclusions below). Three exclusion classes documented: (a) source-grounded-Founders failures — France Université Numérique (Owner-only), openHPI (Owner-only), OpenLearning (Key people only, outside strict-policy allowed source labels), MIT OpenCourseWare ('initiative of MIT' is institutional but the verb 'initiative of' is not within the strict-policy verb-phrase list 'founded by' / 'co-founded by' / 'created by' / 'initiated by' / 'launched by' / 'founding partners'; no `Founders`/`Founder(s)`/`Created by` infobox field either), OpenSAP ('provided by SAP' similarly outside the strict-policy verb-phrase list); (b) own-Wikipedia-article failures — Canvas Network (redirects to Instructure parent); (c) pre-2000 founding-year failures — Stanford Online (per-platform article body 'Stanford Online was founded in 1995 through the Stanford Center for Professional Development'; master-list 'Founded' shows 2006 but per-platform article is preferred — added in cycle 9), Open Universities Australia (per-platform infobox `Established` 1993; master-list 'Founded' shows 2013 but per-platform article is preferred), Saylor Academy (1999, both master and per-platform), The Great Courses (1990, both master and per-platform — added in cycle 9), LinkedIn Learning (1995, both master and per-platform — formerly Lynda.com, rebranded after 2015 LinkedIn acquisition; added in cycle 9). Founded year normalization: each platform's Wikipedia article infobox 'Founded' / 'Launched' field is preferred; where the article lead paragraph and infobox disagree, the per-platform article (lead + infobox) is preferred over the master 'List of MOOC providers' table value. This rule applies symmetrically: it can either pull a row out of the staged set (Stanford Online, Open Universities Australia) when the per-platform year is pre-2000 even though the master-list year is in-range, or quietly override the master-list year for retained rows when the per-platform article disagrees. Three retained-row master-vs-per-platform 'Founded' discrepancies in the staged 13 (documented in cycle 10): (1) Khan Academy — master list 'Founded: 2006' vs per-platform infobox `Launched: 2008`; staged 2008 (per-platform preferred). (2) OpenClassrooms — master list 'Founded: 2007' vs per-platform article internal split (infobox `Launched: 10 November 1999` records the original Site du Zéro entity; lead 'Founded in 2013 by Pierre Dubuc and Mathieu Nebra, OpenClassrooms…' records the OpenClassrooms-brand rebrand); staged 2013 follows the lead's brand-founding framing. The Stanford-Online-vs-OpenClassrooms treatment is intentionally asymmetric: Stanford Online's article has a single 'founded in 1995' statement with no competing rebrand-year framing in the lead (so 1995 wins → row excluded by pre-2000 filter), whereas OpenClassrooms's article lead explicitly says 'Founded in 2013… OpenClassrooms' (so 2013 wins → row retained). (3) Udacity — master list 'Founded: 2012' vs per-platform infobox internal split (`Founded: June 2011` corporate founding vs `Launched: February 2012` product launch); staged 2011 prefers the `Founded` field as the more conventional founding-year sense. Founders normalization: founder names are taken from each platform's Wikipedia article lead paragraph (preferred) or infobox 'Founders' / 'Founder(s)' / 'Created by' field; multiple founders are concatenated semicolon-delimited and alphabetized within a row's cell. Where the founder is an institution rather than an individual, the institution name is given AND must be source-labeled by either an explicit infobox Founders/Created-by field or by a body-text founder verb-phrase ('founded by' / 'co-founded by' / 'created by' / 'initiated by' / 'launched by' / 'founding partners') in the platform's article. The infobox `Owner` field by itself is not sufficient for the Founders cell. Specific source-grounding paths in the staged set: edX 'Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Harvard University' per article lead 'founded by MIT and Harvard' (verb-phrase 'founded by'); FutureLearn — all 12 universities named in the article body's '12 founding partners are: The Open University, University of Birmingham, ...' clause are listed in the staged Founders cell, alphabetized (verb-phrase 'founding partners'); SWAYAM 'Government of India (Ministry of Education)' per article lead 'launched by the Ministry of Human Resource Development… Government of India' (verb-phrase 'launched by'); Wikiversity 'Wikimedia community' per article infobox `Created by` field (infobox path); Shaw Academy 'Adrian Murphy; James Egan' per article infobox `Founders` field (infobox path). Country of Origin normalization: the country of the platform's headquarters per the cited Wikipedia article, normalized as 'United States' (not 'U.S.', 'US', or 'USA'), 'United Kingdom' (not 'UK' or 'U.K.'), and 'Germany' / 'France' / 'Ireland' / 'India' verbatim. One row uses an explicit owner→parent derivation chain because the per-platform article does not state a country directly: Wikiversity's article infobox supplies `Owner: Wikimedia Foundation` and `Created by: Wikimedia community` but no country/HQ; the Wikimedia Foundation Wikipedia article (source_urls[14], added in cycle 10) supplies 'Headquartered in San Francisco, California, United States', which source-grounds the staged Wikiversity Country of Origin = United States. The country distribution in the staged 13-row set: United States 7, Ireland 2, United Kingdom 1, Germany 1, France 1, India 1.
open_questions: 1. Whether MIT OpenCourseWare and OpenSAP should be included by widening the strict-policy verb-phrase list. The current strict list is 'founded by' / 'co-founded by' / 'created by' / 'initiated by' / 'launched by' / 'founding partners'. MIT OCW's 'initiative of MIT' and OpenSAP's 'provided by SAP' are institutional but use different verbs. A v2 could either widen the list (e.g., add 'initiative of' / 'provided by' / 'developed by' / 'operated by') or keep the strict closed list and accept the 2-row exclusion as the cost of strict source grounding. 2. Whether to widen the universe to all 'List of MOOC providers' master-list entries regardless of own-article requirement (clause 1), with rows for entries lacking own articles drawn from the master-list row itself. The current design keeps clause 1 to ensure each row has a per-platform Wikipedia article supplying the cells, which is the standard for this benchmark family. 3. Whether the 2000-2020 founding-year window is the right scope for MOOC-providers-only. Five master-list entries fall pre-2000 under the per-platform-preferred rule: The Great Courses (1990), Stanford Online (1995), LinkedIn Learning (1995), Open Universities Australia (1993), and Saylor Academy (1999); widening the window to 1990-2020 would add all five rows (Stanford Online and OUA would re-enter despite their master-vs-per-platform discrepancies) but loosens the 'modern MOOC era' implicit framing. 4. Whether 'Wikiversity' belongs in the universe at all — Wikipedia's master MOOC-providers list classifies it as MOOC, but Wikiversity's content delivery model is more wiki-based-self-study than course-cohort-based and may not match the colloquial MOOC framing some readers expect. The current design defers to the master list's classification. 5. Whether the per-platform-article-preferred rule for the founding-year filter should be relaxed when the per-platform article and master list materially diverge. Stanford Online's 1995 'founding' refers to the Stanford Center for Professional Development as the institutional precursor; the rebranded 'Stanford Online' platform per se launched around 2006 (consistent with the master list). A v2 could distinguish 'platform launch year' from 'institutional precursor year' and use the former for the filter, which would re-admit Stanford Online (2006). The current design errs on the side of the per-platform article's stated founding year for consistency.
